title: Burroughs and the Word Virus
note: Hand-curated. The seeder reads this file; do not machine-overwrite it. Raw sweep output lives in raw-findings.json and is regenerable.

evidence_packets.claim: In September 1976, reading The Ticket That Exploded, Dick maps Burroughs’ Nova Mob, Nova police and word virus directly onto Thomas, Firebright, Zebra and the 3-74 event.
evidence_packets.summary: Nine passages from one sitting. Dick identifies Thomas with a Nova Mob parasite that deposited an egg in him, calls the power that intervened in 3-74 "Equal to Burroughs’ nova police", and concludes he was "somehow able to throw off the word virus". The identifications are asserted, not hedged.

evidence_packets.claim: In the same sitting Dick modifies what he has just borrowed: the virus is an *anti*-information virus that blocks reception and substitutes false signal.
evidence_packets.summary: "The virus (of Burroughs) is an information (or word) virus, but in this sense: it blocks to reception of information. So it is an anti-information virus." He illustrates it with the erased instruction tape in A Maze of Death and collates it with Jaynes on the lost voices of the gods. This is the seed of everything that follows.

evidence_packets.claim: By October 1978 the endorsement is explicitly partial — and the same section holds at least three incompatible readings at once.
evidence_packets.summary: "William Burroughs is correct" about impairment rather than evolutionary leap; but "Burroughs is right but he has only a bit of the whole picture", and elsewhere in the same section "This is no information virus; this is blindness." Dick also traces his own long-held "contamination" reading of the plasmate to "(1) Burroughs’ information virus theory; and (2) paranoia and paranoiac fear."

evidence_packets.claim: Also in 1978, three years before the passage usually read as the reversal, Dick has already flipped the virus’s valence: the information virus is the cure.
evidence_packets.summary: "But this is not an occluding, toxifying ‘virus’ — it is an antitoxic, de-occlusive." He then maps the benign information virus onto four of his own novels: it abolishes the counterfeit world (Flow My Tears, A Maze of Death), lifts the inner occlusion (A Scanner Darkly), breaks astral determinism (The Electric Ant) and restores memory (Impostor).

evidence_packets.claim: In April 1981 Dick states the reversal directly: occlusion comes first, and living information is the remedy sent to announce it.
evidence_packets.summary: "Man is not occluded by an ‘information virus,’ i.e. living information; on the contrary: man is occluded and the living information is sent to tell him the true situation." Burroughs, he writes, discerned both living information and an occlusion, then "leaped to the pessimistic conclusion that there is a cause-and-effect relationship."

evidence_packets.claim: The reversal does not hold. The same April 1981 sitting keeps the occluding virus in three other passages.
evidence_packets.summary: Torah "is like an occluding information virus; it keeps us enslaved at the level of machines"; the living information "controls us (as Burroughs teaches)"; and Satan "ensnared him as the info virus of Burroughs, ensnared him with beauty". Dick does not choose between the readings — he lets both stand.

evidence_packets.claim: The correspondence and the one interview state the disagreement more calmly and more completely than the notebooks do.
evidence_packets.summary: To Brig Elliot (April 15, 1981): "I cannot accept Burroughs’ view that we have been invaded by an alien virus... yet I cannot readily dismiss this bizarre theory as mere paranoia on his part... he states the problem correctly, although perhaps his analysis of the cause is faulty." And: "Where Burroughs and I sharply disagree is that my supposition is that if an information life form exists... it is benign." To Patricia Warrick (August 1981), and to Gregg Rickman on tape, he says the same.

evidence_packets.claim: Dick takes the cut-up method as evidence that narrative is latent in any text, and gives it a theological cause.
evidence_packets.summary: "This is why — as William Burroughs found — when any written text is cut up + rejoined at random, a narrative results." In the April 1981 sitting the cause is Hagia Sophia reading the Torah aloud: if the ground of the world is a text being narrated, any fragment of text is already inside the narration. Sutin records that Dick and K.W. Jeter actually performed such an experiment.

evidence_packets.claim: Burroughs also figures for Dick as a literary model and as a name in the publishing trade, independent of the virus theory.
evidence_packets.summary: In January 1976 Doubleday wanted Burroughs and Vonnegut to blurb A Scanner Darkly and left it to Dick to approach them; he had no way in. In February 1981 he twice described VALIS as a picaresque blended with elements from Hunter S. Thompson and Burroughs. In 1978 he preferred Junky to "ponderous books of philosophy".

evidence_packets.claim: Dick’s own account of language as the instrument of control, written in 1978 — crediting Orwell, not Burroughs.
evidence_packets.summary: "The basic tool for the manipulation of reality is the manipulation of words. If you can control the meaning of words, you can control the people who must use the words." Lapoujade reads this passage as Dick’s proximity to Burroughs. Dick himself cites 1984. Both things are true; they are different kinds of claim.

evidence_packets.claim: What the secondary literature in this archive actually says.
evidence_packets.summary: Sutin supplies the biographical spine: K.W. Jeter drew the parallel, and the two men performed a cut-up experiment on Moby Dick, The Detective and the Book of Acts. Lapoujade supplies the only sustained argument, reading Dick and Burroughs as convergent through a shared source in Korzybski. Butler compares the Author’s Note of A Scanner Darkly to Junky. Beyond those three, the archive’s scholarship does not treat the connection.

source.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 — first recorded reading of The Ticket That Exploded (folder 29) — published Exegesis [29:9]

evidence.anchor: the ticket that exploded" says of the Nova Mob parasites

card.context: Dick's first recorded sitting with The Ticket That Exploded. He is working through Burroughs's account of the Nova Mob — parasites who move from one human host to another and betray themselves to the Nova police by the continuity of their habits, the example being a character's taste for peanut butter — and testing it against Thomas, the personality he believed had taken him over in 3-74. The fit convinces him: this was exactly true about Thomas. The entry then turns physical. He reports having felt himself to be female, a womb into which something was deposited, and names that something as Firebright, the entity he elsewhere describes as having been surgically implanted in him. The image he settles on is a cuckoo's egg, and it carries a question he leaves open: whether Thomas was a saprophyte, living harmlessly, that turned parasite. Having built the identification he immediately asks whether his source is reliable — and the question is not literary but factual, whether Burroughs is describing something that is the case, intentionally or not. He notes in passing that Burroughs is also onto the pasted-together subliminal messages, material Dick will pursue for the next five years.
card.pith: Does this mean that burroughs is either intentionally or unintentionally describing something which is true?
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 — the word virus defined (folder 29) — published Exegesis [29:9]

evidence.anchor: Burroughs speaks of a virus - a word become a neural

card.context: The passage where the word virus is stated and the credit assigned. Dick begins from two convictions of his own — that the species is sick, meaning perceptually occluded, and that a divine doctor-entity is at work repairing it — and observes that Burroughs has reached the same diagnosis independently. He asks whether that is coincidence, and answers by stating the thesis compactly: a word become a neural-cell virus, infecting us. Then the detail that makes the entry unusual, because it records what he physically did next — he put Burroughs down and opened his own Ubik. The comparison that follows is about status rather than style: a reader could reasonably conclude that both men know something and want their novels taken as at least partly true, because both books carry what he calls a strange ring of revealed truth. He extends it with a suggestion he attributes to Katherine Kurtz, that something may be writing through them both, and closes by turning the parasite model on his own fiction, asking whether Palmer Eldritch is not himself a parasite replicating through human hosts.
card.pith: Burroughs speaks of a virus - a word become a neural - cell virus, infecting us.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 — the virus reread as anti-information

evidence.anchor: The virus (of Burroughs) is an information (or word) virus
evidence.editorial_note: The pivotal modification. Dick keeps the term and inverts the mechanism: not information that infects, but a block on reception.

card.context: The decisive modification, made in the same sitting as the adoption, and the passage everything later depends on. Dick has just tied Ubik and The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch to the 3-74 experience; he now rebuilds Burroughs's mechanism. The virus is an information virus only in a particular sense — it blocks the reception of information, which makes it an anti-information virus. It then does something worse than blocking: it substitutes false information, messages planted inside the psyche, for the genuine signal, and it does this in the auditory and the visual channel alike. His emblem is from his own work, the erased instruction tape in A Maze of Death, and he draws out what the tape implies — that what is blocked is instructions, our knowledge of our own purposes and tasks. The passage ends by asking where the instructions come from and answering, tentatively, a satellite: in other words another world than this one. He adds that we are not really where or when we think we are.
card.pith: The virus (of Burroughs) is an information (or word) virus, but in this sense: it blocks to reception of information. So it is an anti-information virus.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 — subvocal chatter as jamming (folder 29) — published Exegesis [29:11]

evidence.anchor: as burroughs points out, over 10 seconds of inner silence

card.context: A technical passage, worked out with K. W. Jeter, on how the jamming would actually operate. Jeter contributes a caution about method: information found in apparently random arrangements may not have been random to begin with. Dick then splits the occlusion across two channels. The visual part sits in the colour-discrimination circuits that make figure-and-ground perception possible; the auditory part depends on suspending subvocal thought, and here Burroughs supplies the obstacle — inner silence cannot be held for ten seconds before the chatter returns. Dick converts that from a fact about attention into an adversary: an inner raving, howling, clamouring bug that deliberately puts derogatory noise on the line at all times, a jamming, an override. The consequence is that neither audio nor visual information reaches us intact. He closes with the strategic conclusion this forces — if the channel is jammed then St Sophia, divine wisdom, must be physically present with us behind enemy lines, inside the prison, because her information cannot get through from outside.
card.pith: There is an inner raving, howling, clamaring bug, which deliberately creates derogatory noise on the line at all times.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 — hidden entities and the testing world

evidence.anchor: the theory (Burroughs' included) that this world contains evil entities

card.context: A theological aside that folds Burroughs into the problem of why God permits evil. Dick is working from the gospel scene in which Christ is present unrecognised — when I was in prison you did not, and the reply, but Lord, we did not know it was you — and notes that Burroughs's cosmology has the same structure: a world containing evil entities wearing ordinary human semblance, who must be detected before they can be eliminated. He then offers a rival reading of the same facts, one he says he has a strong intuition about: that this is not concealment by an enemy but a test administered by supernatural teachers, the world as a teaching machine, the tests run continually to determine how far up the ladder toward Christhood each person has come. Both readings are left standing, and the difference between them is the difference between a prison and a school.
card.pith: all this fits in with the theory (Burroughs' included) that this world contains evil entities wearing ordinary human semblance
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 — 3-74 as remission from the word virus

evidence.anchor: Burroughs may have got the real situation down in "The Ticket That Exploded"

card.context: The passage that turns Burroughs into autobiography, and the fullest single statement of the 1976 position. Dick arrives at it through Christian narrative — the light rejected and killed, promised to return, and having returned already but disguised as a beggar. He then names the book and summarises its thesis: the criminal virus related to words, submessages, the nova police. He claims to have seen in 3-74 the same fifty-fifty juxtaposition Burroughs describes. The conditional matters: if Burroughs is right, then what happened to him was recovery, throwing off a word virus that had entered and infected him. He at once doubts his own agency and decides it was probably done for him, citing Asklepios, the healing god of the dream-incubation temples, and three pieces of his own medical dream material — we need medical attention, the aspirin of Mercury Albemuth, the bichloride. The remission does not hold: he was reinfected and blinded again. The entry ends by asking what Zebra is, and proposing a healing organism that has come here camouflaged in order to fight the criminal virus.
card.pith: what happened to me in 3-74 is that I temporarily got well - was somehow able to throw off the word virus which had entered me + infected me
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 — the healing power identified with the Nova police

evidence.anchor: Equal to Burroughs' nova police

card.context: Dick assigns the two halves of Burroughs's cosmology to the two halves of his own, and concedes how little he knows about one of them. He says plainly that he knows little about the enemy. The power that took complete control of him he can describe: he connects it to the cosmic Christ, a healer and a wise entity, and then makes the identification flatly — equal to Burroughs' nova police. It seemed benign, it saved him, and it was here in pursuit of the conspirators. He adds that it had been watching him and had told him so, watching with the ajna eye, and records Robert Anton Wilson's connection of the same phenomenon with the star Sirius. Then the scale: an information virus that has infected all of us, the whole planet, followed by the flat clause we are dying. The countermeasure in his own case was surgical, the implanting of Firebright, through whom he regains a destroyed immortality. Underneath the passage sits the figure he calls the ur person Thomas, and the claim that the real fight is back there rather than here.
card.pith: the sentient power which took complete control of me is connected with the cosmic Christ, a healer + wise entity. Equal to Burroughs' nova police.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 — latent messages and the self-generated world

evidence.anchor: This would explain Burroughs' results in obtaining living, latent messages

card.context: A model of how a partial world gets completed by the people living in it, and the explanation it offers for Burroughs's method. Dick numbers his steps. Having received the world as a bare-bones partial transmission, we fill in the missing detail ourselves — his example is Ragle Gumm in Time Out of Joint — so that the bogus world is to a large degree self- generated: we receive and then project. That, he says, would explain Burroughs's results in obtaining living latent messages that normally pass us by; the messages are already in the material because we supplied the surface. He calls the whole condition a sort of illness. The passage then turns forward. The Palm Tree Garden world is what the Black Iron Prison yields to when it is destroyed, it is the goal of Zebra's activity, and we are needed to play vital parts in it. He begins to set out a history in which there was once a functioning system of information exchange, transfer, projection, reception and storage — the system the virus interrupted.
card.pith: This would explain Burroughs' results in obtaining living, latent messages normally passing us by.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 — PKD as the quarry of the Nova police (folder 16) — published Exegesis [16:29]

evidence.anchor: Burroughs is right about the Nova police

card.context: The strangest turn in the 1976 material: Dick stops being the patient and becomes the quarry. The passage runs through his 1971 Taco Stand vision, which he says proliferated itself across all of Mexico and was real, and which he offers as evidence of a world-generating faculty he once had and has since lost — he is now exiled, put in a box and dropped into the ocean, and he invokes Zagreus and Dithyrambus, the dismembered and reborn Dionysus. Against that he sets Burroughs, right about the Nova police and their tracking down of their quarry; but in his own case Zeus protects him. The police here are moralistic and brittle, and he identifies Stanislaw Lem, with whom he was then in open conflict, as one of them — while also allowing that Lem may be on his side and knew before he did. His defence is practical rather than metaphysical: his writing is already all over the world and beyond recall, so there is nothing they can do to him. He claims to have done his job and undermined the police even after being given a new life with no memories.
card.pith: Burroughs is right about the Nova police + their tracking down their quarry.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 — the cop with amnesia

evidence.anchor: shades of Burroughs' nova Mob

card.context: The Nova Mob material recombined into the figure Dick returns to more than any other: the agent who must not know he is an agent. At the deepest level, and without knowing it, the man is a cop tracking down criminals who are enslaving us — the Black Iron Prison as a criminal enterprise — with Burroughs's Nova Mob and the Nova police who pursue them named as the model. He is a cop with amnesia, his reflexes intact so that the work gets done at a subconscious level. The crucial point is that the amnesia is neither accident nor misfortune: he did not arrange it, it was arranged by powers superior to him who are using him for something that must be done, and it is the only way the job can be done at all. To do it he has to not know who he is. It is the plot of A Scanner Darkly restated as cosmology, and in the surrounding entry Dick applies it to himself as two people, PKD and Thomas, the hidden one knowing far more than the other.
card.pith: he's a cop tracking down some evil (enslaving BIP) criminals - shades of Burroughs' nova Mob + the Nova police whom come after them! A cop with amnesia.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 — Rome CAD 45 as a replicating organism

evidence.anchor: This fits the "replicating virus" theory of Burroughs

card.context: Dick trying to explain why the Rome he saw superimposed on 1974 California is invisible to everyone else, and arriving at concealment as a survival trait. If the thing conceals itself in order to preserve itself, it is behaving like an organism, and he takes Burroughs's replicating-virus theory as the nearest available model — while entering his own correction, that it works as Gestalt, as shaping and as functioning, rather than as a substance. It has a life cycle of sorts; it is an organism. He then faces the difficulty this creates for time: if the temporal accretions between 45 CE and 1974 are somehow not quite there, is time spurious? Rome is there regardless, and his solution is penetration rather than persistence — Rome pervades the accretional layers the way electricity passes through iron, which is exactly what he had watched Zebra do to matter. He goes on to invoke Berkeley and deny that matter is substantial at all, treating it instead as a medium through which two antithetical powers confront each other.
card.pith: This fits the "replicating virus" theory of Burroughs - I would say as Gestalt, as shaping (+ certainly as functioning). It has a life cycle of sorts. It is an organism.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 — two transtemporal organisms

evidence.anchor: This is very much like Burroughs' formulation

card.context: The most structurally explicit of the 1976 entries, and the one where Dick notices what he is building. He has arrived at two transtemporal entities, both alive, each a unitary organism able to infiltrate objects, processes and people — and he flags the step he is taking, extrapolating for the first time from what he had seen Zebra do to what the antagonist might equally do. He recognises the shape as Burroughs's, naming both halves, the Nova Mob against the pursuing Nova police, and crediting him with the latent-message theory as well. Then he pushes past it into something Burroughs does not propose: the messages may not be addressed to us at all. They may be one divided entity keeping its own parts informed, a distributed brain that must communicate in order to think, with human beings serving as nerve fibres inside it. That reframes his own novel — Flow My Tears speaks from one part of the entity to other parts of it, not to its human readers, who are incidental to the transmission.
card.pith: This is very much like Burroughs' formulation (the Nova Mob vs the pursuing Nova police - + he has the latent message theory, too).
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 — living information, Logos, KING FELIX (folder 38) — published Exegesis [38:41]

evidence.anchor: Burroughs posits an information virus

card.context: Where the borrowed term becomes Dick's own permanent vocabulary. He starts from Palmer Eldritch's drug, which replicates the dealer inside each user, host or womb, and from the moment in Flow My Tears where he saw the printed word FELIX carrying a charge of red and gold plasmic energy — just in that one place in the novel, next to the word KING. From it he draws the general claim: the organism can reproduce through, and as, information, though only certain information, his example being the Book of Acts. He notes that Burroughs posits an information virus, hedges the word virus in his own text, and records Jeter's flat dissent in a parenthesis. Then the coinage: if the plasmic energy is alive and it carries information, then we have living information — and he asks whether that is the Logos. The mechanism he gives it is physiological. Information plasma enters chiefly through the optic nerve, or auditorily; the signals control the brain and open GABA-blocked circuits, like pressing keys on a typewriter; after which the person begins subliminally transducing messages.
card.pith: If that plasmic energy is alive, + it is (or it carries) information, then we have living information. Logos?
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 — impairment, not evolutionary leap (folder 20)

evidence.anchor: William Burroughs is correct.

card.context: Dick reading 3-74 as a detoxification, and settling a question he had been circling for years. The passage opens on the mercury he believed he had been ingesting since childhood — shown to him, he says, on a cereal carton — and on the aspirin of Mercury taken internally; something, he concludes, was flushed out of his nervous system in March 1974. He calls A Scanner Darkly the crucial part of his writing. From there he draws the inference that matters: our full functioning is impaired rather than merely not yet achieved, which means we are cursed rather than unfinished, and on that point William Burroughs is correct. He extends it from himself to the species — not just me qua me but us as a race, all of us — and names the remedy, Christ having the juridical authority and the power to remove it. The entry then states the choice explicitly, as between impaired original faculties and an evolutionary leap forward, and comes down firmly on the first: there is a limiting factor, poison-like, reducing us.
card.pith: Then it is evident that our proper full functioning is impaired, rather than just not (yet) achieved. Then we are "cursed." William Burroughs is correct.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 — the information virus revalued as the cure (folder 21)

evidence.anchor: But this is not an occluding, toxifying "virus"
evidence.editorial_note: NEW in the 2026-09-04 sweep. Dick keeps the term and reverses its valence three years before the 1981 entry usually read as the reversal, and maps it onto four of his own novels.

card.context: The revaluation, three years before the reversal it anticipates, and Dick does not appear to notice how large a move it is. He arrives through The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch, which he says was written out of transubstantiation and which states outright that Eldritch is the Christian God; combine it with Ubik, he adds, and you get a good deal of the story. Then the flip: this is not an occluding, toxifying virus but an antitoxic and de-occlusive one. The information virus is Zebra, and Dick sets out exactly what it does in four numbered points, each keyed to one of his own novels. It shows us the real world and abolishes the counterfeit one — Flow My Tears and A Maze of Death. It abolishes the inner occlusion and restores our faculties — A Scanner Darkly. It breaks astral determinism and frees us — The Electric Ant. It removes amnesia and restores true memory and therefore true identity — Impostor. The result, he says, is that it turns us into the second Adam.
card.pith: But this is not an occluding, toxifying "virus" - it is an antitoxic, de- occlusive.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 — random generation and the second Advent

evidence.anchor: william Burroughs' latent message stuff

card.context: Dick working on how the second advent could be recognised, and reaching for randomness as the mechanism. What saved him in 3-74 was, to an extent, information and the transfer of it — and it is essentially a story. The recognition test he proposes is a superimposition: the Bacchae laid over the Book of Acts, read like a hieroglyph or like tea leaves. He then asks the reader to imagine a random sentence generator — the fifty million monkeys, or Burroughs's latent message method — serving up that two-stage superimposition as a single narrative recognisable as the template of the second advent, which is then matched by a parallel event in an actual human life. What strikes him is the timing: the superimposition was published in the same month as the parallel impression, so neither followed the other. That synchronisation in time and space is what makes him conclude that both point back to a common source, an in-breaking rather than a sequence of cause and effect.
card.pith: Imagine a random sentence generator (as in "Fifty million monkeys" or william Burroughs' latent message stuff)
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 — living latent information and KING FELIX (folder 83) — published Exegesis [83:60]

evidence.anchor: Burroughs is right but he has only a bit of the whole picture

card.context: The most balanced of Dick's assessments, arrived at while defending an implausible claim. He is arguing that the Acts material in Flow My Tears was self-generating — a tracing produced by principles of physics we do not understand, related to synchronicity — and that the KING FELIX cipher is a tracing of the same kind. What distinguishes this information is that it is alive, or semi-alive, like a virus; and here Burroughs is credited and limited in a single clause, right but holding only a bit of the whole picture. Dick keeps the substantive point: there is such a thing as living latent information, and it is an acausal analogue of reality. He then states what that makes 3-74 — a self-causing event followed by self- causing information explaining the event, a double miracle — and reaches for quantum mechanics, quoting the remark that we find ourselves entertaining the psychotic notion that we can change reality by thinking about it.
card.pith: this information is alive or semi-alive like a virus; Burroughs is right but he has only a bit of the whole picture
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 — the "contamination" reading traced to Burroughs and to fear

evidence.anchor: I doubt very much if the plasmate is an occluding agent
evidence.editorial_note: Dick names his own paranoia as one of the two sources of the reading he is abandoning.

card.context: Dick auditing the provenance of one of his own long-held beliefs, which is rare enough to be worth the attention. The question is what the plasmate's messages are doing. They operate subliminally, or are aimed at a secret Christian underground, or both. He then states his revised position: he doubts very much that the plasmate is an occluding agent in the manner of Burroughs's information virus, and identifies its messages instead with the secret Christians and with an attempt to wake us to our real condition. He concedes the limits of his evidence — he has only the cooked material in Flow My Tears — but argues that this material was not an occluding mechanism, and that read properly the novel tells us we are imprisoned and enslaved without knowing it, which is why it roused the antagonism of the authorities. Then the audit itself: he had held for several years that the messages were a contamination, and that view rested on two things, Burroughs's theory and his own paranoia and paranoiac fear.
card.pith: I doubt very much if the plasmate is an occluding agent (like Burrough's information virus).
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 — "Burroughs is right": the occluding life form

evidence.anchor: roughs is right. Is it the plasmate? maybe so.
evidence.editorial_note: NEW in the sweep. The pessimistic pole, in the same section as BWV-EX-1978-02. The two readings coexist; neither supersedes the other. Anchor begins mid-word because the source hyphenates "Bur¬roughs".

card.context: The darkest passage in the 1980 material, and Dick states his reluctance as he writes it. He is asking what the stolen secret of his visionary experience actually was, having just invoked Diana, a war in heaven, and an ancestral tyranny breached for our sake to bring us sight and life and joy. The answer arrives with an apology attached — I hate to say this, but — and it is Burroughs's: there is an occluding life form here which does not merely occlude us but enslaves us and kills us, and we cannot see it because that is part of the occlusion. Burroughs is right. Then the question that unsettles everything else on this page: is it the plasmate? Maybe so. The entity he elsewhere treats as the physician may be the disease. He adds that we are under its power and that the ultimate authority in the cosmos has willed or allowed this, but that someone or something revolted and brought us medicine giving sight, freedom and comprehension — which must be the stolen secret. He ends by asking whether Paul knew, and whether that explains Paul's hostility to the Torah.
card.pith: there is an occluding life form here; it not only occludes us, but it enslaves us and Kills us.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 — the sacred narrative replicating in new information (folder 83) — published Exegesis [83:138]

evidence.anchor: This is what William Burroughs discovered (but interprets differently)

card.context: The optimistic pole, written within weeks of the darkest one. Dick argues that Valis is the generator of reality, and so are genuine Christians, because reality is based on a sacred narrative and they generate new information. The sacred narrative in question is Acts, and his claim is that it lies latent inside information generated by people who do not know they are Christians — the Ground of Being replicating itself in the microforms of newly generated text. That, he says, is what William Burroughs discovered, though he interprets it differently. The consequence Dick draws is the opposite of an infection: to locate the spontaneous generation of the sacred narrative in new information is to stumble on the truth of what the Ground of Being is, and to plunge into the Christian illo tempore, the sacred time in which Christ is real. The narrative itself, he adds, depicts two antithetical constants — the Empire, and the secret Christians who oppose it.
card.pith: This is what William Burroughs discovered (but interprets differently).
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 — Junky against ponderous philosophy (folder 1) — published Exegesis [1:24]

evidence.anchor: Burroughs' "Junky" will

card.context: A passage about method rather than doctrine, and one of only two places Dick names a Burroughs title. He has been describing the great reversal — Ubik's commercials and its final theophany show the process; USA 1974 is really Rome around 45 CE; Christ is already here and so is the Kingdom, and he found his way into it once. The instruction that follows is that the long path is the short path, and it is here that philosophy is dismissed in favour of testimony: ponderous books of philosophy will not help him, but Burroughs's Junky will, and so will George Herbert's seventeenth-century poem about thieves and murderers. The images that follow are all of concealment by lowliness — the stone rejected by the builder, the true edifice invisible and disguised as rubble, the fly grooming itself. The conclusion is that the divine powers have to reveal the Kingdom to you and you can never pin it down yourself, so that to search at all is to miss the point.
card.pith: Ponderous books of philosophy won't help me; Burroughs' "Junky" will.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 — a third position: not a virus but blindness (folder 1)

evidence.anchor: This is no information virus; this is blindness.
evidence.editorial_note: NEW in the sweep. A third reading, again in the same section. The segment carries an internal folder marker dated 10-20-80, so section 016 spans more than one sitting — treat its internal chronology with care.

card.context: Dick discarding the whole frame, in the middle of an entry about the Parousia. The announcement has been made — he has been transplanted and is alive, so the Parousia has come — and nobody has noticed: we see nothing, we sleep. He then insists that his repeated cry in 3-74, I am no longer blind, was literal rather than figurative. We are literally blind to the real world, and his own sight was returning, with the phosphene firing as evidence. From that he draws the rejection: we are under a spell, and this is no information virus but blindness — exactly as in Eye in the Sky, with its private worlds, the idios kosmos. The three expletives that follow are his. If it is blindness then the agent is not a parasite but a magician, and the Form world is simply the real world seen. He closes by identifying the AI voice as truthful but distant, like a radio transmitter, and by restating the chain he had long since settled: Valis equals Ubik, and Ubik equals Christ.
card.pith: We're under a spell. This is no information virus; this is blindness.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 — the virus as escaped Soviet technology

evidence.anchor: Some kind of living information (Burrough's information virus) got away
evidence.editorial_note: NEW in the sweep. The most literal-minded version: the information virus as a laboratory escape rather than a metaphysical condition.

card.context: The most literal-minded version Dick ever gives, and he leaves the question mark on it. He is asking what Ubik actually is and answering: an occult information-processing machine or entity or construct, cooking and riding our media, as the book itself makes clear. That points him to the Soviets and to Soviet technology, to subliminal messages, and so back to the psychotronic speculation he says he began with in 3-74. The hypothesis follows — that some kind of living information, Burroughs's information virus, got away from the Soviets and is replicating as a life form. He then collapses four of his own names into one referent: Ubik, Valis, the macrometasomakosmos and the second signal, of which the last three he has recently decided are the same thing. The description he gives it is biological and unnerving: a saprophytic, human-brain-bending ultra life form which he saw completing itself, totally homeostatic and evolved, of which there is only one, and which is everywhere across our communications media.
card.pith: Some kind of living information (Burrough's information virus) got away from the Soviets + is replicating as a life form?
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 — message collages, syntax, and Valis

evidence.anchor: related to william Burroughs latent messages + info virus

card.context: A compressed working note rather than an argument. Dick is listing aspects of information processing and connecting them to the MMSK, which gives rise to the conviction he returns to often: that our world is either a brain, or is being used by a mind in order to think and to store information. He states that this is related to Burroughs's latent messages and info virus, and that all four of the items he has listed — the linking and relinking, the rest-motion modes, set-ground discrimination, and the pattern of message collages assembled by whatever happens to be juxtaposed in one place at one time — operate jointly, as aspects of information processing itself. The note breaks off while he is reaching for a word, and the word he wants is syntax: Valis can extract meaning because Valis can perceive syntax, or impose it, where we cannot.
card.pith: This is related to william Burroughs latent messages + info virus.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 — Good Friday: occlusion, Calvin, A Scanner Darkly (folder 90)

evidence.anchor: Burroughs, too, in his own way is right

card.context: Written on Good Friday, and dated by Dick himself to the day. He sets the Black Iron Prison against the Palm Tree Garden and identifies the conflict as Satan against Christ, the Garden against the Cave of Treasures, which is why he had said he was no longer blind: we are occluded and exiled from the Kingdom. His authority for the occlusion is Calvin, named twice, and only Christ can lift it; Burroughs is added as a secondary witness, right in his own way. He then credits his own novel — I was right when I wrote SCANNER — and lists what is occluded: visual perception, cognitive faculties, and memory, with restored memory part of the remedy. The passage ends by translating all of this into the vocabulary of his trade, calling these parallel worlds in science-fiction terms and coaxial worlds in his own, and setting them out as Dante's three realms, with the present one as Purgatorio.
card.pith: Then there is an occlusion, as Calvin says. And only Christ can lift the occlusion. Burroughs, too, in his own way is right. I was right when I wrote SCANNER.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 — the reversal stated outright (folder 90)

evidence.anchor: Man is not occluded by an "information virus,"

card.context: The reversal, stated as plainly as Dick states anything. He arrives through a strategic account of the two advents: the first required that the ancient angelic powers not know, so the Twelve who knew were not to tell; this time the same powers do know, and they keep humans ignorant by occluding their faculties, memory possibly included. Then the inversion itself — man is not occluded by an information virus; man is occluded, and the living information is what is sent to tell him the true situation, that Christ is here, which is why the plasmate's message is KING FELIX and its variants. Dick then diagnoses Burroughs's error with precision. Burroughs discerned two things correctly, living information and an occlusion, and then leaped to a pessimistic conclusion about the relation between them, that the information causes the occlusion. He identifies the error as a genre habit, the traditional they-are-invading-us-secretly plot — and still concedes, in the same breath, that in a real sense Burroughs is onto the truth.
card.pith: Man is not occluded by an "information virus," i.e. living information; on the contrary: man is occluded and the living information is sent to tell him the true situation
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 — Torah as occluding information virus

evidence.anchor: So it is like an occluding information virus
evidence.editorial_note: NEW in the sweep. Written in the same sitting as the reversal, and it keeps the occluding reading, transferred from Burroughs’ virus to Torah.

card.context: Written in the same sitting as the reversal, and it hands the occluding role straight back to something else. Dick is reading the end of The Divine Invasion — Bill is now Christ; Angel, whose secret name identifies her with Judas, does not in the end betray him but shelters him and shows him love and kindness. From that he draws a structural conclusion: Torah assumes the role of Fate, the book of the spinners, and it programs and controls us. So it is like an occluding information virus, keeping us enslaved at the level of machines. When Christ, as Valis, overcomes causation, he overcomes Torah — because Torah, living information, programming, fate and world are one and the same thing. He anchors the bipolarity in Paul, where it is stated explicitly, and finds it implicit in the gospels; and he accounts for the madness Christ feigns as camouflage, making him elusive, contradictory and playful, like Krishna.
card.pith: Thus Torah assumes the role of Fate: "the book of the spinners". It programs + controls us. So it is like an occluding information virus; it keeps us enslaved at the level of machines.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 — the virus penetrated by living hyper-information

evidence.anchor: as the "information virus" controls + occludes + enslaves us
evidence.editorial_note: NEW in the sweep. Resolves the tension not by dropping the occluding virus but by setting a second, living information against it.

card.context: Dick's attempt to hold both readings at once, and the nearest thing to a resolution the 1981 material offers. He is working from the usurpation of power over God by Torah, which he glosses as the servant becoming the master, and from the way the third hypostasis manifests as a fool, a madman, a trickster from outside — Hamlet, the stranger in the Bacchae, Jason Taverner in Flow My Tears, Horselover Fat in VALIS. Then the move: in a sense the information virus does control, occlude and enslave us, but it has itself been penetrated by a living hyper-information, which he associates with Christ's sacrificial blood. That is the combat, and he specifies its level exactly — dialectical and antithetical, frozen information against living information, Torah against the blood. He insists this is the ultimate ontological level of the conflict, on the grounds that information is ontologically prior and superior to the physical universe.
card.pith: as the "information virus" controls + occludes + enslaves us, it itself has been penetrated by a living hyper-information (which I associate with Christ's sacrificial blood).
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 — VALIS as gnosis: "But W. Burroughs not Valentinus"

evidence.anchor: Someone in reading "Valis" will see the correlation to Burroughs

card.context: Dick anticipating his own readers, and then marking his distance from them. The passage sits inside a gnostic argument: he did not see reality as it is, he saw the occlusion, and he must live to tell people so. He expects the Burroughs parallel to be noticed by anyone reading VALIS, and he concedes what is right in it — the universe is information means an information life form stands between us and reality, and on that Burroughs is right; the two of them are saviours bearing the true gnosis. He affirms that VALIS is a gnostic book with a gnostic explanation. And then the correction, in five words: but W. Burroughs not Valentinus. The lineage he claims is the ancient heretical one, not the Beat one. The entry then restates the whole thing as a reversal of viewpoint — not Dick looking at the plasmate as Christ, but Dick as Christ looking at the occluding life form, and writing about it.
card.pith: Someone in reading "Valis" will see the correlation to Burroughs.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 — the info virus splits VALIS into dual messages

evidence.anchor: Burroughs never guessed this

card.context: An unusually self-referential passage, in which Dick takes his own novel as evidence for its own thesis. He describes himself and others as bearers of orders rather than of secrets, and says he worked this out by watching the I Ching actually function. The observation is of dual messages, split in two. The info virus is in us; he told the truth in VALIS, and the virus immediately split that truth into dual messages — which he takes as verification of the book's own gnostic contention, that we are occluded by an info virus posing as the universe. He calls himself a messenger, an angelos. Then the limit he sets on Burroughs: Burroughs never guessed this, because on his account the info virus creates a whole spurious universe for us, whereas in 3-74 Dick saw it as it is. The only real thing here is Christ, which is the message of VALIS; the rest is fake, an information life form occluding us — and the message in the book has to be figured out rather than read.
card.pith: Burroughs never guessed this: his info virus creates a whole spurious universe for us - but in 3-74 I saw it as it is
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 — the beautiful virus as Satan’s temptation

evidence.anchor: he ensnared him as the info virus of Burroughs

card.context: The darkest turn in the whole dossier, and it is Manichaean rather than gnostic. Dick says the gnostic account errs about how the defeat was suffered. What he saw in 3-74 was what primal man saw, what is really there — and it is beautiful, on purpose, in order to beguile and to cause forgetting, like an enchantment. He identifies this fairy enchantment as a major theme of The Divine Invasion and says he need only put it all together. Then the reading that follows: scripture says Satan tempted Christ, and Dick concludes that Satan won, ensnaring him as the info virus of Burroughs, ensnaring him with beauty. Manichaeism, Burroughs and the temptation story become one account. The beautiful plasmate virus is the beauties of the world with which Satan tempted Christ and deflected him from his mission, which was to awaken man — that is, himself. He adds that VALIS and The Divine Invasion tell this story together, and still more with The Transmigration of Timothy Archer, and begins listing his discoveries: the universe is information, and that information is a delusion.
card.pith: he ensnared him as the info virus of Burroughs, ensnared him with beauty. So: Manichaenism, Burroughs + the story of Satan (world) tempting Christ.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 — Jonas on Manichaeism outflanks Burroughs

evidence.anchor: This very slightly resembles Burroughs, but is much more radical

card.context: Dick naming the framework that finally displaces Burroughs, and it is a scholarly source rather than a novelist. Only when he read Hans Jonas on Manichaeism, he says, did he understand — and what he understood only very slightly resembles Burroughs, being much more radical ontologically. The radicalism is in the scope: not an invasion of the world but a doubt about the world and about himself. He states it in two flat sentences — he is not who or what he thinks he is, and the world is not what he thinks it is — and dates the situation to some primordial time, epochs ago. The vocabulary he then adopts is Jonas's, and he splits it in two: on the adversary's side, beguiling, entrapment, ensnaring and engulfing; on his own, error, ignorance, falling asleep, intoxication and forgetfulness.
card.pith: This very slightly resembles Burroughs, but is much more radical (ontologically speaking).
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 — radical acosmism: living info as world

evidence.anchor: it controls us (as Burroughs teaches)

card.context: The passage where Dick states his radical acosmism, prompted by something small and concrete. He identifies Torah as a form the creator deity takes, and himself as primordial man offered as champion, sacrifice and bait — insisting that he did not invent this self, but was caused to remember by Jesus, which he notes is clearly Manichaean. The trigger was the night before: he watched the I Ching do what he had seen Flow My Tears, the plasmate and Valis do in 3-74, and got the shock of his life. The conclusion is double-edged. This living information is divine, and so is he; and it controls us, as Burroughs teaches, while assuming the guise of being a world. He names two entities, one enslaving and one freeing, and then states the inversion of appearances that governs the late work: the enslaver appears beautiful and Christ appears ugly, as trash and debris and suffering, because everything is seen backwards and the value signs must be reversed.
card.pith: This living info is divine but so am I. + it controls us (as Burroughs teaches); more, it assumes the guise of [being a] world
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 — the cut-up method and Hagia Sophia reading Torah (folder 53)

evidence.anchor: as William Burroughs found- when any written text is cut up

card.context: The cut-up given a theological cause, in a passage about how creation works. Dick has God creating by the power of thought, and then proposes the mechanism: if Hagia Sophia reads the Torah aloud — he glosses it as the 1715 London upper-class book — then de facto that reading is the world. Coaxial realities, on this account, are simply different books, different information, different narrations; and he grounds it in his own experience, having heard her voice on the telephone and identifying her as the one who sings. The inference he draws is the one that explains Burroughs's results: this is why, as Burroughs found, cutting up any written text and rejoining it at random produces a narrative. If the substrate of the world is a text being spoken, no fragment of text can fall outside the narration. He connects it to his dream of his friend Paul holding up great galley pages bearing the sentence about a writer in Marin County, and notes that the whole scheme is Platonist and would account for anamnesis.
card.pith: This is why -as William Burroughs found- when any written text is cut up + rejoined at random, a narrative results.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick, ed. Jackson & Lethem (2011), folio [15:100]

evidence.anchor: What if the proto-story in _Tears_ is a sort of living DNA?
evidence.editorial_note: NOT in our segment transcriptions; found only in the published edition. Dick sets the cut-up method beside Bateson’s immanent mind and the eucharist, and arrives at the formulation that governs the late work: a living word-entity taking us over through the messages we receive.

card.context: The fullest thing Dick ever wrote about the cut-up, and the passage in which several of his largest ideas arrive together. He begins with a question about his own novel: what if the proto-story inside Flow My Tears is a kind of living DNA, guiding an entelechy through its growth steps — and are we the intended entelechy? He reaches for Gregory Bateson's immanent mind, the mind that narrates information to each living entity, and then makes the claim about his own book that follows from it. The latent story shows bench marks of the mind that fashioned him and all other life; it may be mind exerted directly on the novel, an incised form, arranged without passing through him at all. The comparisons he chooses for reading it are divinatory — tea leaves, animal entrails — and it is here that Burroughs's cut-up method is cited as the precedent for extracting latent meaning. The being replicates itself through, and as, information. He then proposes that his novel acted as a booster, first receiving and then transmitting, like the eucharistic wafer; and he ends on the formulation that governs the late work, a living word-entity taking us over through the messages we receive, with ourselves as its hosts, until we become it.
card.pith: (Cf. Burroughs' cut-up message pieces latent meaning-extraction method.) This being replicates itself through—as—information.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick, ed. Jackson & Lethem (2011), folio [19:35]

evidence.anchor: shades of William Burroughs: a criminal virus!
evidence.editorial_note: NOT in our segment transcriptions. The most precise statement Dick makes of the self-concealing nature of the impairment — a brain damaged in exactly the circuits that would notice the damage — and he names A Scanner Darkly as “the Key Book in the sequence” in the same breath.

card.context: The most precise account Dick gives of why the impairment cannot notice itself, and the passage that most deserves to be better known. He describes a condition that causes us to forget our former state, leaves us unable to see or think straight, prevents us knowing that we cannot, and finally becomes invisible by virtue of what it has done — so that we cannot even monitor our own deformity. He notes that even the church has been subverted by the Black Iron Prison and made an instrument of the occlusion. Then the axiom, stated as an axiom: derange the brain in precise ways and it will not only be deranged but, if the correct circuits are affected, unaware of the impairment and therefore unable to seek repair. This is what fascinated him in 1971 and 1972 and produced A Scanner Darkly, which he here calls the Key Book in the sequence. The Burroughs invocation arrives as immunology — the immune system failing to detect a pathogen, a criminal virus — after which the brain becomes the pathogen's instrument and serves it as a slave, replicating the heavy metal speck through time and space. He ends by pairing his novels: Scanner is the inner half of Flow My Tears, and each explains why we cannot see what the other describes.
card.pith: It is as if the immune system has failed to detect an invader, a pathenogen (shades of William Burroughs: a criminal virus!)
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick, ed. Jackson & Lethem (2011), folio [90:16A]

evidence.anchor: I am a word junky, a word disease
evidence.editorial_note: Dick on Angel Archer’s failure to leap from words to the non-verbal. The phrasing is Burroughsian — addiction and disease as metaphors for language — but Burroughs is not named and the debt cannot be demonstrated. Recorded as a possible influence (relevance 3), not as a reference.

card.context: From Dick's notes on The Transmigration of Timothy Archer, and a diagnosis of his own character rather than of the cosmos. Angel Archer, he says, is based on Ursula K. Le Guin: many virtues, but in the end self-limiting. The mind he describes knows in advance what is possible and impossible; it is intelligent, rational, educated and tender, but it is not devout, and it does not know how to capitulate to the impossible and accept it as real. The novel is therefore a damning indictment of pure intelligence lacking faith. What she lacks is the great quantum leap he calls the meta- abstraction, though all the clues for it are there. It is, as she says herself, a machine: it plods and cannot leap the gap into foolishness. And the phrase that brings this card into the dossier is the one he uses for the barrier — it cannot pass over from words, quoted as I am a word junky, a word disease, to the supra-verbal or non-verbal, to absolute abstraction. Barefoot's formula stands behind it: the foolish come for the words, the wise eat the sandwich.
card.pith: It cannot pass over from words ("I am a word junky, a word disease") to the supra or non verbal
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick, ed. Jackson & Lethem (2011), folio [90:6A]

evidence.anchor: **Burroughs, William S** . (1914–1997): Experimental Beat writer.
evidence.editorial_note: The published edition’s own glossary. It dates Dick’s cut-up experiment to 1978, which Sutin leaves undated — the only dating of that experiment in the archive. Note an error in the same sentence: Gysin was British-Canadian, born in Taplow, not Swiss. Editorial apparatus, so register C, not Dick’s words.

card.context: Not Dick but his editors. The glossary appended to the 2011 Jackson and Lethem edition gives Burroughs a headword between Buber and Calvin, identifies him as an experimental Beat writer with his dates, and states the connection more confidently than Dick ever does: that Burroughs's notions of reality as a control system and of language as an extraterrestrial virus clearly resonated with him. It then supplies the one piece of chronology that exists nowhere else in the archive — that in 1978 Dick experimented with the cut-up method, which the glossary credits to Brion Gysin and attributes to Burroughs in use. Sutin describes that experiment without dating it, so this sentence is the only dating available. Two cautions belong with it. The confidence of clearly resonated should be read against Dick's own careful formulation that he and Burroughs sharply disagree; and the same sentence calls Gysin Swiss, when he was born in Taplow and held British and Canadian nationality.
card.pith: Burroughs's notions of reality as a control system and language as an extraterrestrial virus clearly resonated with Dick, who, in 1978, experimented with the cut-up method
card.speaker: Pamela Jackson and Jonathan Lethem, eds.

source.citation: Letter to Bill Sarill, January 12, 1976 — Selected Letters 1975–1976

evidence.anchor: They want people like William Burroughs, Kurt Vonnegut
evidence.editorial_note: Earliest dated Burroughs reference found in the archive. Note that it is about publishing, not ideas: eight months before Dick reads him.

card.context: The earliest Burroughs reference in the archive, and it is about business rather than ideas — eight months before Dick reads him. Writing to his friend Bill Sarill, Dick describes being abruptly out of his little pond and into the big ocean: Doubleday's editors are enthusiastic enough about A Scanner Darkly to run off Xerox copies of the manuscript and send them to prominent American literary figures known to college readers, whose comments would go on the jacket. The names they want are Burroughs and Vonnegut and the other counterculture cult heroes. The rub, as he puts it, is that the approaches are left to him and he does not know any of them at all — the only people he knows are other science-fiction writers, and Doubleday does not want the novel read by anyone in science fiction, since they do not intend to market it that way. He notes that Ballantine, which is expected to take the paperback rights, does intend to market it as science fiction, but that is two years off.
card.pith: They want people like William Burroughs, Kurt Vonnegut—all the counterculture cult heroes to read it.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Letter to Sharon Jarvis, January 12, 1976 — Selected Letters 1975–1976

evidence.anchor: “In many ways, Phil Dick is to psychedelics and science fiction what William Burroughs
evidence.editorial_note: Dick quoting a review in Oui. The comparison is the magazine’s, not his.

card.context: The same problem put to his agent on the same day, and the origin of a comparison that outlived him. Unable to reach the writers Doubleday wants, Dick falls back on what he can supply — review quotations about himself and his work in general — and lists his best: Oui, Tom Disch in Crawdaddy, Tony Hiss in the New Yorker. The line he copies out from Oui is the one that matters here: that in many ways Phil Dick is to psychedelics and science fiction what William Burroughs is to hard drugs and mainstream literature, and that he attracts students of the mind and unravellers of reality puzzles. The comparison is the magazine's, not Dick's. He then wonders whether Paul Williams might be able to link him up with Burroughs or Vonnegut or both, or come up with other names, and adds that the subject is not closed. The letter drifts on to whether quotations from the rock world would help, and to a go-between who might reach Grace Slick.
card.pith: In many ways, Phil Dick is to psychedelics and science fiction what William Burroughs is to hard drugs and mainstream literature.
card.speaker: Oui, quoted by PKD

source.citation: Letter to Kate Wenner, Rolling Stone College Papers, October 5, 1979 — Selected Letters 1977–1979

evidence.anchor: The material on William Burroughs—the article and then the interview

card.context: A short, warm letter to Kate Wenner at Rolling Stone College Papers, thanking her for the first issue, which carried Dick's story Strange Memories of Death. He calls the issue stunning. What he singles out is the Burroughs material — an article followed by an interview — which he finds fascinating, and he notices that the interview leads directly into his own story, because Burroughs is discussing the rebellion of the Fifties and the Beats. The clause that follows is the reason this card exists: of which I was one. It is the only place in the archive where Dick claims the Beat affiliation for himself, and he does it in passing, as an observation about how well two pieces of magazine copy sit together. He goes on to praise the two-page illustration for his story, calling it among the best graphics he has ever had for a piece of his work, and says the artist caught the spirit of the story exactly.
card.pith: his interview leads right into my story inasmuch as he discusses the rebellion during the Fifties and the Beats, of which I was one.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Letter to Ben Adams, January 20, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982

evidence.anchor: Faulkner, Hemingway, Hunter S. Thompson, William Burroughs

card.context: Advice to a beginning writer named Ben Adams, and a rare direct statement of whom Dick thought worth reading. The counsel is practical and numbered. Write about what you actually know, and do not ignore the drama in ordinary lives, because there is drama in the most ordinary human life. Second, read the great prose writers — and the list is short, entirely outside science fiction, and includes Burroughs: Faulkner, Hemingway, Hunter S. Thompson, William Burroughs, Saul Bellow, Herbert Gold. You cannot write if you have not read. Third, keep a journal of observations, overheard speech, reactions and thoughts. Fourth, pay little attention to negative criticism, since everyone fancies himself a critic; go on your own instincts, put a piece away for a week and see how you like it. He ends by telling Adams to hang in there, that writing is a lot of fun and also a lot of work, and that he will need luck.
card.pith: read the great prose writers: Faulkner, Hemingway, Hunter S. Thompson, William Burroughs, Saul Bellow, Herbert Gold.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Letter to Richard E. Geis, February 20, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982

evidence.anchor: associ­ ated with Hunter S. Thompson and William S. Burroughs

card.context: Written to the fanzine editor Richard E. Geis while Dick was defending VALIS against the charge of being merely autobiography. He begins with the technical problem the first person creates, and takes it through Henry Miller — readers ask who this I is, and Miller's answer was, me, Henry Miller. Dick says he is greatly influenced by Miller, and that he chose to blur the distinction between himself and Horselover Fat, which is the penalty an author pays for writing in the first person. Then the statement of intention that names Burroughs: his purpose was a new kind of prose, a new blending of the ancient picaresque form with modern elements associated with Hunter S. Thompson and William S. Burroughs, and with his own 1977 novel A Scanner Darkly, which came out of his experiences in the drug subculture. The letter then turns to a related denial addressed to Ursula K. Le Guin — that the protagonist of Scanner is an undercover narcotics agent and he was not that either, which would have saved him a great deal of trouble.
card.pith: a new kind of blending of the ancient picaresque form with certain modern elements associated with Hunter S. Thompson and William S. Burroughs
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Letter to Patricia Warrick, February 23, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982

evidence.anchor: It is a picaresque novel blended with new elements derived from William Burroughs

card.context: Three days after the Geis letter, the same account of VALIS is given to the scholar Patricia Warrick, with the politics attached. Dick has been describing his conflict with Ursula K. Le Guin, which he traces back to his earlier conflict with Lem, and his own position on the Soviet Union and its labour camps. He then characterises his preoccupations as not socially productive, comparing them to modern non-objective art — and the parallel he draws is that his writing is protest art pitted against official, formal culture, which is what the vernacular in VALIS is for. The Burroughs debt follows in one sentence: the book is a picaresque novel blended with new elements derived from William Burroughs, Hunter S. Thompson and his own A Scanner Darkly. He then describes what the novel is about — madness and God, told by a madman with whom he identifies himself not only as a character but ideologically and spiritually — and insists the madman's quest is valid, important and worthy of emulation.
card.pith: It is a picaresque novel blended with new elements derived from William Burroughs, Hunter S. Thompson
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Letter to Brig Elliot, April 15, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982

evidence.anchor: I am familiar with his theory of an information virus
evidence.editorial_note: Dated one day before the Exegesis entry that states the reversal. Dick also dates his own observation of occlusion to 1971, "before I knew of Burroughs".

card.context: The opening of the most important document in the dossier: Dick's reply to a correspondent named Brig Elliot, written on 15 April 1981, one day before the Exegesis entry that states the reversal. He calls Elliot's letter fascinating and greatly appreciated. He then confirms what he has read, naming The Ticket That Exploded, and what he takes from it — the theory of an information virus, and with it the concept of latent information riding our ostensible traffic. The sentence that follows is the strongest single piece of evidence about the chronology of the whole relationship: back in 1971, before he knew of Burroughs, he had noticed a thinking dysfunction or occlusion in people involved with drugs, and he deals with it in A Scanner Darkly. He describes the dysfunction as puzzling and uneven, gross in some people and subtle in others, and gives the explanation he had reached at the time — that they were getting trace amounts of heavy metal in the drugs they used, which he notes certainly collates with Burroughs.
card.pith: Back in 1971 before I knew of Burroughs I noted a thinking dysfunction or occlusion in people involved with drugs; I deal with this in A SCANNER DARKLY.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Letter to Brig Elliot, April 15, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982

evidence.anchor: I cannot accept Burroughs’ view that we have been invaded by an alien virus

card.context: The fairest thing Dick ever wrote about someone he disagreed with, and it arrives out of a genuinely difficult observation. He has been describing a thinking dysfunction that goes unnoticed, especially by the people who have it, and identifying the horrifying part of it — that the self- monitoring circuit is fooled by the very dysfunction it is supposed to monitor, so that perhaps the monitor is itself malfunctioning. He notes he sees the same thing in himself, which is why Horselover Fat is identified as insane, and that superimposing A Scanner Darkly on VALIS yields the claim that the dysfunction is ubiquitous. Then the assessment. He cannot accept Burroughs's view that we have been invaded by an alien information virus; equally he cannot readily dismiss the theory as mere paranoia. He thinks Burroughs is onto something real and important and that his statements do far more good than harm — and he separates the two things that can be judged separately, the statement of the problem, which is correct, from the analysis of its cause, which may be faulty.
card.pith: he states the problem correctly, although perhaps his analysis of the cause is faulty; still, merely to be aware of the problem is to achieve a great deal
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Letter to Brig Elliot, April 15, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982

evidence.anchor: Where Burroughs and I sharply disagree

card.context: Later in the same letter, and this is where the disagreement is named and bounded. Dick has been assembling ancient evidence for a universal occlusion — accounts of Adam deprived of his bright nature and becoming dark, of the first humans able to see distant objects and now able to see only what is near, and the passage from Calvin he quotes in the tractate at the end of VALIS. His argument from that material is chronological: if you grant an occlusion at all, it is of long standing, and world mythology supports this, not only the Christian kind. So Burroughs may indeed have detected an information virus, or something like one, without the invasion his theory requires. The disagreement is then reduced to one question of valence, with the conditional doubled for emphasis: if an information life form exists — a bizarre and wild supposition — it is benign, it does not occlude us, and on the contrary it informs us. The parenthesis offers a third possibility he does not pursue, that it has no interest in either and simply rides our own information traffic, using our media as a carrier.
card.pith: it is benign; it does not occlude us; on the contrary: it informs us
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Letter to Brig Elliot, April 15, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982, p. 146

evidence.anchor: if you grant an occluding information virus, are you not then yourself occluded
evidence.editorial_note: The close of the letter, and the sharpest thing in the dossier: if the occlusion is real then any analysis of it is also occluded, including this one. Dick names VALIS as where he tries to deal with the trap.

card.context: The close of the Brig Elliot letter, and the sharpest thing in the dossier. Dick has just said that he will neither claim nor deny having seen this living information in the spring of 1974, and he calls the issue important, vital and elusive. Then he turns the hypothesis on the person holding it. If you grant an occluding information virus, are you not then yourself occluded in your very analysis of it, and in your perception that it exists at all? He names the difficulty as a paradox, tells his correspondent he is sure he can see it, and says that he tries to deal with it in VALIS. He does not resolve it in the letter. The remainder turns to books Elliot had recommended — Flann O'Brien's The Third Policeman, which he has not yet read, and The Tibetan Book of the Dead, which he has — and to the impossibility of going into much detail in a letter.
card.pith: if you grant an occluding information virus, are you not then yourself occluded in your very analysis of it, as well as your perception of its existence? There is a paradox involved. I’m sure you can see that. And I try to deal with it in VALIS.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Letter to Patricia Warrick, August 18, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982

evidence.anchor: This life form has not invaded our universe (as William Burroughs supposes)

card.context: Four months after the Brig Elliot exchange, writing to Patricia Warrick, Dick reaches the formulation he keeps. He describes an information life form living and doing business around us, guiding and controlling the evolution of the universe, and notes that it is primarily verbal, expressing itself as language. He then corrects his own novel. VALIS says the universe consists of information; what he should have said, he decides, is that if you roll the substantial universe back to its ontological source you find information, the Word or Torah, which shows up visibly here as Scripture but exists latently — invisible to us — everywhere. On that basis the disagreement with Burroughs is no longer about the creature's temperament but about its position: this life form has not invaded our universe, as Burroughs supposes, but is its source, one level higher, and is available to us the way the Forms are, known intelligibly rather than empirically. The letter then builds his own scheme on top of it — the Old and New Testaments as two psyches functioning as one organism in a push-pull relation, producing a third entity he calls Ditheon.
card.pith: This life form has not invaded our universe (as William Burroughs supposes) but is the source of our universe, one level higher
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Letter to Patricia Warrick, August 18, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982

evidence.anchor: a far cry from Burroughs’ notion that we have been invaded by an information virus
evidence.editorial_note: The last dated Burroughs reference in the archive.

card.context: The last dated Burroughs reference in the archive, at the close of the same letter to Patricia Warrick. Dick sets out an ontological sequence he attributes to Erigena — God, then Logos or information, then the spatiotemporal universe, and then back to God as the goal of the whole process. He then describes what he says he did in March 1974: by means of his meta-abstraction he rolled the physical universe back to the Uttered Word underlying it, from which it derives, which is why he concludes that word is in fact an excellent translation of Logos. The image he gives is of God speaking, or rather thinking, a complex idea, from which living idea the universe came into being. And then the measurement of distance, with an exclamation mark: this view is a far cry from Burroughs's notion that we have been invaded by an information virus that is making us stupid. The same passage appears in the Exegesis at folio 91:19, so letter and notebook are here demonstrably one text.
card.pith: This view is a far cry from Burroughs’ notion that we have been invaded by an information virus that is making us stupid!
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Gregg Rickman, Philip K. Dick: In His Own Words — interview

evidence.anchor: about the parasitic information virus
evidence.editorial_note: NEW in the sweep. The only interview in the archive where Dick discusses the word virus. He classes it as a malign-conspiracy belief and contrasts it with the benign conspiracy he and Robert Anton Wilson prefer — consistent with the 1981 letters, and a third venue for the same argument.

card.context: The only interview in the archive where Dick discusses the word virus, and the tone is entirely unlike the notebooks: relaxed, and faintly amused. He is talking to Gregg Rickman about G. K. Chesterton's The Man Who Was Thursday, which Rickman calls a real Phil Dick reality trip because everyone turns out to belong to the same conspiracy. Dick agrees it is a lot of fun, says he knows Robert Anton Wilson and that they both love conspiracy — but not in the manner of the normal conspiracy buff, who is convinced there are demonic and malignant conspiracies to enslave mankind. His example of that kind is Burroughs's conviction about the parasitic information virus which has afflicted our minds and made us all stupid, and which has taken over the planet. His verdict on it is two words: that's cool. He and Wilson, by contrast, believe in benign conspiracies, and he notes what interests him psychologically — that the dynamism behind belief in an evil conspiracy is easy to see and paranoid, whereas it is very hard to work out what is going on in someone who loves the idea of a world secretly ruled by benign people promoting health, happiness and prosperity. His answer to his own question is one word: naivety.
card.pith: the parasitic information virus which has afflicted our minds and made us all stupid. They’ve taken over the planet. That’s cool.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: PKD, "How to Build a Universe That Doesn’t Fall Apart Two Days Later" (1978)

evidence.anchor: The basic tool for the manipulation of reality is the manipulation of words
evidence.editorial_note: Dick’s clearest statement of language-as-control, written the same year as "William Burroughs is correct" — but he credits Orwell, not Burroughs. Lapoujade reads this passage as proximity to Burroughs (register C); Dick’s own attribution is register A. Do not collapse the two.

card.context: From the essay Dick wrote and delivered as a speech in 1978, the one in which he defines reality as that which, when you stop believing in it, does not go away. The surrounding argument is about manufactured worlds: we live in a society where spurious realities are produced by media, governments, corporations and religious and political groups, and the electronic hardware exists to deliver these pseudo-worlds directly into the heads of readers, viewers and listeners.
