He worries about what his eleven-year-old daughter is being taught by television, and about miscuing — a programme made for adults, watched by a child, half or perhaps all of it misunderstood. Into that argument comes the sentence this card exists for: the basic tool for the manipulation of reality is the manipulation of words, and if you can control the meaning of words you can control the people who must use them. The authority he names for it is George Orwell and Nineteen Eighty-Four, not Burroughs. He then adds the second method, controlling perception rather than language, because comprehension follows perception — which is why he thinks television's power over young minds is so vast, words and pictures being synchronised.
card.pith: The basic tool for the manipulation of reality is the manipulation of words. If you can control the meaning of words, you can control the people who must use the words.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions: A Life of Philip K. Dick (1989)

evidence.anchor: He called attention to the similarities between Phil
evidence.editorial_note: THE key biographical finding. Sutin identifies the "KW" of the 1976 Exegesis entries as K.W. Jeter, reports that Jeter drew the Burroughs parallel, and records that Dick and Jeter performed their own cut-up experiment on Moby Dick, Roderick Thorp’s The Detective and the Book of Acts — the same Acts material Dick elsewhere claims generated itself in Flow My Tears.

card.context: The single most useful paragraph of biography in the dossier. Sutin is describing K. W. Jeter's role after the two men resumed their friendship in late 1976, following a three-year break that began when Dick suspected Jeter might be a government agent. A former antiwar activist in the Socialist Workers Party, Jeter was not drawn to the religious theories Dick had built out of 2-3-74, but he knew how to stoke the theoretical fires and add complexities on top of Dick's own — the gadfly role, played to perfection. It is Jeter who called attention to the similarities between Dick's novels and Burroughs's, specifically an invading alien virus occluding human faculties, with the note that for Burroughs the virus is language. That identifies the KW credited throughout the September 1976 Exegesis entries. Sutin then records that the two men performed their own Burroughs-influenced cut-up experiment, scrambling texts from Roderick Thorp's The Detective, Melville's Moby Dick and the New Testament Book of Acts. He adds that Jeter worked a graveyard shift at the Orange County Juvenile Hall, which left him available for the late- night calls in which Dick interrupted his Exegesis to test the latest possibilities — and that Jeter, speaking to the interviewer Andy Watson, stressed that Dick always kept a minimum hypothesis in reserve.
card.pith: He called attention to the similarities between Phil’s novels and those of William Burroughs-such as an invading alien virus occluding human faculties (for Burroughs, the virus is language).
card.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions (1989)

evidence.anchor: Jung, Kant, William Burroughs, the Bible
evidence.editorial_note: Sutin places Burroughs in Dick’s lifelong reading. Note the tension with Dick’s own statement to Brig Elliot that he did not know Burroughs before 1971–76; Sutin gives no date for the reading.

card.context: Sutin placing Burroughs among Dick's reading, in a passage about the breadth of it. The context is Dick's early formation: he had read Finnegans Wake several times in his early twenties, and the range of his reading throughout his life was virtually limitless, running from technical papers on physics to Binswanger's daseinsanalyse, and taking in Jung, Kant, William Burroughs, the Bible, the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Bhagavad Gita. Sutin immediately distinguishes reading from influence: asked about influences on his work, Dick would name Stendhal, Flaubert and especially Maupassant before he got round to any science-fiction writer, crediting Maupassant and James T. Farrell with teaching him how to structure the stories he sold for a living in the early fifties, over seventy of them in three years. The passage carries no date for the Burroughs reading, which is the reason it cannot settle the chronological question, and it should be read against Dick's own statement that in 1971 he did not yet know of Burroughs.
card.pith: Throughout his life the range of his reading was virtually limitless, from technical papers on physics to Binswanger’s daseinanalyse to Jung, Kant, William Burroughs, the Bible, the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Bhagavad Gita.
card.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions (1989)

evidence.anchor: A student once asked William Burroughs if he believed in life after death
evidence.editorial_note: Sutin uses a Burroughs anecdote to frame Ubik’s central question. This is the biographer’s comparison, not Dick’s.

card.context: Sutin using Burroughs to frame Ubik — the biographer's comparison, not Dick's. The context is the novel's central undecidability. An explosion casts the characters into a transformed reality that may or may not be controlled by Pat Conley, or Runciter, or Hollis, or someone or something else; Runciter believes he knows which, and composes a graffito to tell Joe Chip so. Sutin's point is that Runciter cannot be sure, since Joe Chip's face turns up on a coin in his pocket. It is here that he introduces the anecdote: a student once asked Burroughs whether he believed in life after death, and Burroughs asked back how you know you are not dead already. Ubik, Sutin says, offers no solution to Burroughs's question because there is none — but it does offer Ubik itself, whose name he glosses from the Latin for everywhere, and which may be enough for half-lifers to get by on. He adds that it is not easy to come by, requiring hard work and a kind of religious faith.
card.pith: A student once asked William Burroughs if he believed in life after death. Burroughs asked back: How do you know you’re not dead already?
card.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions (1989)

evidence.anchor: William Burroughs employs a junkie patois
evidence.editorial_note: Sutin judges Dick’s drug dialogue more accurate than Burroughs’.

card.context: A judgement on style, and it goes against Burroughs. Sutin is discussing the antidrug theme of A Scanner Darkly and the surprising position Dick took in 1973, writing to the Department of Justice to offer help in the war against illegal drugs, calling drug abuse the greatest problem he knew of, and proposing to dedicate the novel to Attorney General Richard Kleindienst — a remarkable exception to his otherwise implacable opposition to the Nixon administration. Sutin notes that in daily life Dick was less adamant, smoking the occasional joint or bowl of hash. He then argues that the novel nails down the hazy, twisting weirdness of sixties doper dialogue perfectly, and makes the comparison: in The Soft Machine and The Wild Boys, Burroughs employs a junkie patois that is part forties Times Square, part private eye, part laconic Beat Burroughs — vivid and sharp, but not the way it actually sounded. What it did sound like, Sutin says, is Ernie Luckman's scheme for smuggling hashish carved into the shape of a man.
card.pith: William Burroughs employs a junkie patois that is part forties Times Square, part private eye, part laconic Beat Burroughs. Vivid and sharp, but not the way it sounded at the time.
card.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions (1989)

evidence.anchor: if, say, William Burroughs and Thomas Pynchon

card.context: Sutin on the cost of genre classification, with Burroughs as the control case. He has just quoted Dick on his own purpose — that the core of his writing is not art but truth, and that his corpus is one long ratiocination about an irrational, mysterious reality which helps a certain kind of sensitive, troubled person who will not blunt their own intimations. Strict categories, Sutin says, worked against him. A Scanner Darkly and VALIS were marketed as science fiction, but had Burroughs and Pynchon respectively written them they would have been received as mainstream literature; the difference is categories, not quality. He runs the argument in the other direction as well, with Borges: Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius, about an imaginary planet that gradually becomes our world, would have been shelved as science fiction had Dick written it. He then offers Pierre Menard as a way out of the categorical maze, since the same text produced by a different consciousness necessarily has a different effect.
card.pith: They were marketed as SF, but if, say, William Burroughs and Thomas Pynchon, respectively, had written them, they would have been mainstream.
card.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: David Lapoujade, Worlds Built to Fall Apart: Versions of Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: On this point, Dick is rather close to William S. Burroughs
evidence.editorial_note: The most sustained scholarly treatment of the connection in this archive. Lapoujade quotes Burroughs’ "Word begets image and image is virus" (Nova Express) beside Dick’s "How to Build a Universe" passage.

card.context: The core of the only sustained scholarly treatment of the connection in this archive. Lapoujade has been arguing that for Dick the left hemisphere is dedicated to the programming of the psyche: the brain literally becomes a servo-mechanism, adapting its own plasticity to conform to alternatives preestablished by linguistic and numeric algorithms. He quotes Dick's own sentence about the manipulation of reality being the manipulation of words, and then makes the comparison — on this point Dick is rather close to Burroughs, for whom the words of a language are tools for taking control of brains and taking over their capacity to construct realities. He states Burroughs's thesis directly, that the human brain is infected by a virus which spreads by means of language as its carrier, and quotes Nova Express: word begets image, and image is virus. He then follows Burroughs further, into the idea that humanity is infected by its own deteriorated image, loving the idealised image of its inhumanity more than itself, with poverty, hatred, war, bureaucracy and insanity as symptoms of the human virus.
card.pith: On this point, Dick is rather close to William S. Burroughs, for whom the words of a language are tools used for taking control of brains and taking over their ability to construct realities.
card.speaker: David Lapoujade

source.citation: David Lapoujade, Worlds Built to Fall Apart

evidence.anchor: This proximity between Dick and Burroughs stems in part from their readings of Alfred Korzybski
evidence.editorial_note: Lapoujade’s causal claim: Korzybski is a shared source rather than Burroughs being a source for Dick. The archive contains no direct evidence either way for Dick’s Korzybski reading; treat as register C.

card.context: Lapoujade's causal claim, and the most contestable thing on this page. Having established the resemblance between Dick and Burroughs on language as control, he explains it not as influence but as convergence: the proximity stems in part from their readings of Alfred Korzybski, whose work describes how the use of language blocks the creativity born of relations at the level of nonverbal experience. He sets out the mechanism — the structure of language tacitly imposes the rules of an old, bivalent, Aristotelian logic on the analogical relations of the right hemisphere — and concludes that we need to be wary of language because its logic exerts control over thought and the images it generates enclose the mind in an abstract world. He then extends the argument to machines, which on this account participate in spreading the virus. The claim should be read carefully here: the archive holds no direct evidence that Dick read Korzybski, and the essay Lapoujade quotes credits Orwell.
card.pith: This proximity between Dick and Burroughs stems in part from their readings of Alfred Korzybski
card.speaker: David Lapoujade

source.citation: David Lapoujade, Worlds Built to Fall Apart

evidence.anchor: the propagative power of a virus

card.context: Lapoujade on proliferating artifacts, and the moment when copies stop being copies. He is cataloguing Dick's fakes — simulacra and androids; the recreated Lincoln and Stanton of We Can Build You, as human as the originals; the synthetic toads and sheep of Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?; Molinari in Now Wait for Last Year, using replicas of himself from parallel worlds as spare bodies. The Burroughs comparison supplies the mechanism by which this spreads: as in Burroughs, the trash has the propagative power of a virus, and like a virus it carries a sickness with it, the malady of an artificial reality that spreads until it becomes the only reality. Little by little, Lapoujade argues, the proliferation of these images gains enough power to constitute entire worlds — which is the step he considers most characteristic of Dick, and the reason the fakes matter more than their individual fakery.
card.pith: As in Burroughs, the “trash” has the propagative power of a virus
card.speaker: David Lapoujade

source.citation: David Lapoujade, Worlds Built to Fall Apart

evidence.anchor: There are no soft drugs in Dick
concepts: The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch

card.context: Lapoujade on drugs as an instrument of control rather than of escape. The argument arrives from media and advertising, which appropriate the external world behind billboards and glowing screens and are equally interested in appropriating the internal world of the psyche — the real objective being to control brains the way drugs do, since whoever controls the transmission of information controls what gets called reality. Hence the claim about Dick: there are no soft drugs in his work, only hard drugs that attack the brain directly and take control of it, as in Burroughs. That, Lapoujade says, is why drugs become a religion in Dick, a religious experience, inverting Marx's formula that religion had been the opium of the people. His case in point is The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch, where two drugs circulate, sold by two dealers described as rival divinities — the first a drug of communion in which users merge with Barbie-like dolls to escape the Martian colonies, a Host that delivers them into a standardised world controlled by the dealer.
card.pith: There are no soft drugs in Dick. There are only hard drugs that attack the brain directly and take control of it, as in Burroughs.
card.speaker: David Lapoujade

source.citation: David Lapoujade, Worlds Built to Fall Apart

evidence.anchor: cooperatives and bureaucracies that Burroughs established

card.context: A structural parallel drawn from Naked Lunch rather than from the Nova trilogy. Lapoujade has been distinguishing the analogical from the digital: the analogical circulates between worlds, while the digital is sealed inside a single one by the translational power of its codes, and he reads Dick's ecological, cosmological sense of communication as a profound vitalism. He then finds Dick arriving independently at a distinction Burroughs had already drawn — between cooperatives and bureaucracies. Cooperatives are founded on the cooperation of individuals and their ability to share common realities. Bureaucracies require a parasitic extraction in order to feed: they never create anything of their own, but graft themselves onto existing activities and claim a share, in the manner of a tapeworm. He quotes Burroughs directly on the point, that bureaus cannot live without a host, being true parasitic organisms.
card.pith: Dick rediscovers the distinction between cooperatives and bureaucracies that Burroughs established in _Naked Lunch_
card.speaker: David Lapoujade

source.citation: Andrew M. Butler, Philip K. Dick (Pocket Essentials, rev. ed.)

evidence.anchor: Burroughs’ testimony about his own sickness
evidence.editorial_note: Butler compares the Author’s Note of A Scanner Darkly to Burroughs’ prefatory testimony in Junky.

card.context: Butler reading the Author's Note of A Scanner Darkly, and using Burroughs to place it. The Note, he says, sees the drug users as playing children who were punished for playing, and who did not know the dreadful consequences of their experimentation. Butler observes that Dick included himself among them, and that the scenes in the rehabilitation centre likely draw on his own experience — so the novel is not an anti-drugs tract. Equally it is hardly an advertisement for drug taking, and the comparison he reaches for is Burroughs's testimony about his own sickness, and the word to the wise that forms the health warning to Naked Lunch. He then makes a separate point about genre: despite its near-future setting the novel is barely science fiction, and he notes the evidence that the United States colluded in the opium trade to help capitalism unbalance south-east Asian communism, with some of that heroin finding its way home.
card.pith: Compare this to William S Burroughs’ testimony about his own sickness and the word to the wise which forms a health warning to _Naked Lunch._
card.speaker: Andrew M. Butler

evidence.anchor: belonged to William Burroughs, the millennium belongs to Philip K. Dick
evidence.editorial_note: Reception rather than argument: Burroughs as the writer Dick is measured against. The same line is reprinted in the fanzine Simulacrum Meltdown 3, there in the present tense ("belong to William Burroughs").

card.context: Reception rather than argument, included because it shows what the pairing came to mean after Dick's death. Erik Davis's line, written for Details, was picked up as a jacket endorsement and reprinted for years — here on the Oxford edition of Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, where it sits immediately after the closing lines of Deckard's narration, and again in the fanzine Simulacrum Meltdown, there in the present tense. Burroughs functions in it as the writer against whom Dick's stature is measured, and the structure of the claim is succession rather than influence: the seventies and eighties belonged to Burroughs, the millennium belongs to Dick. It is worth setting beside the Oui review Dick had copied out for his agent in 1976, which used the same pairing to make a much smaller claim — that Dick was to psychedelics and science fiction what Burroughs was to hard drugs and mainstream literature.
card.pith: If the ’70s and ’80s…belonged to William Burroughs, the millennium belongs to Philip K. Dick.
